steps.say: Bruises of the brain gather at the front and the temples, where the skull base is roughest. The brain slams forward into bone, then rebounds backward, so one blow makes two bruises. These bruises can swell larger over the next day or two, which is why a dip in consciousness demands a repeat scan.
steps.tx: **Cerebral contusions** (brain bruises) cluster at frontal and temporal poles from **coup-contrecoup** (strike and rebound) impact against the skull base. Each forms a **blossoming contusion** (swelling bruise) over **24 to 48 hours** (twenty four to forty eight hours), so **repeat CT** (second head scan) is mandatory when consciousness dips, since an early reassuring scan can hide a growing bruise.

vis.alt: Illustration of traumatic brain injury showing frontal coup and occipital contrecoup contusions, with a microscopic inset showing diffuse axonal shearing and axonal retraction swellings.
vis.caption: Coup-contrecoup contusions at the poles with diffuse axonal shearing shown inset. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Some severe injuries leave the first scan looking almost normal, yet the patient stays deeply unconscious. The damage is at the microscopic level, where twisting forces have torn the wiring across the whole brain. A later MRI with blood-sensitive sequences reveals tiny bleeds where the fibres snapped.
steps.tx: **Diffuse axonal injury** (widespread wiring tear) comes from high-speed twisting that leaves the victim deeply unconscious while the first CT looks oddly normal. Blood-sensitive **MRI susceptibility sequences** (bleed-revealing scans) later show microbleeds at the **grey-white junction** (cortex wiring border), corpus callosum and dorsolateral midbrain, where fibres twisted and snapped.

steps.say: Pathologists grade this wiring injury in three stages, from the surface down to the brainstem. Surface spots alone carry the best outlook, while spots in the great bridge between hemispheres are worse. Lesions reaching the brainstem carry the gravest prognosis of all.
steps.tx: **Adams grading** (axonal injury scale) runs from **grade 1** (one) grey-white junction lesions to **grade 2** (two) corpus callosum involvement to **grade 3** (three) dorsolateral brainstem lesions. **Brainstem** (vital-centre stalk) lesions carry the worst prognosis, so MRI-adapted Adams grading stratifies both expected recovery and the intensity of neurocritical support offered.

steps.say: Concussion is different from all of these structural injuries. The scans are normal because nothing is torn or bleeding; the brain is simply stunned. Doctors diagnose it at the bedside from headache, fogginess, unsteadiness and trouble recalling what just happened after a blow to the head.
steps.tx: **Concussion** is a **functional injury** (stunned but structurally normal brain) with no CT or routine MRI abnormality, diagnosed clinically. Typical features are headache, fogginess, imbalance and **delayed recall** (trouble remembering events) after biomechanical energy transfer to the brain, and the label needs symptoms, not scans, because imaging stays normal by definition.

steps.say: After a concussion, recovery follows a ladder with at least a full day on each rung. The patient rests, then takes on light activity, then training, then full play, stopping at any return of symptoms. A second blow before recovery finishes can cause catastrophic brain swelling in teenagers.
steps.tx: **Return to play** (sport resumption ladder) follows a stepwise protocol with at least **24 hours** (twenty four hours) per stage plus medical clearance before contact resumes. Any **second impact** (repeat blow) before recovery risks catastrophic **second-impact syndrome** (rapid fatal swelling), especially in adolescents, so same-day return is never permitted.

steps.say: Most concussion symptoms settle within weeks, but a few patients are still foggy and unsteady beyond a month. For them, hiding in a dark room makes things worse, not better. Supervised exercise, neck treatment and balance therapy bring recovery faster than prolonged rest.
steps.tx: **Post-concussion syndrome** (lingering fog and imbalance) beyond **4 weeks** (four weeks) in adults needs supervised **active rehabilitation** (graded exercise programme) with **vestibular therapy** (balance retraining). Prolonged dark-room rest worsens outcomes, so persisting headache, dizziness and concentration trouble should trigger referral, not continued isolation.

steps.say: A patient with broken long bones who becomes confused and breathless a day later may be showing fat blocking the brain vessels, not a head injury. Tiny pinpoint bleeding spots on the skin give the game away. The MRI has a starry pattern that looks nothing like ordinary trauma.
steps.tx: Marrow fat released by long-bone fractures can shower the brain, giving coma with low oxygen and pinpoint skin spots that imitate a primary axonal injury. MRI shows a **starfield pattern** (scattered bright dots) rather than contusions, and the fracture-to-coma interval plus **petechiae** (tiny skin spots) point to **fat embolism** (marrow fat blocking vessels), not direct brain trauma.

steps.say: Seizures can follow a severe head injury, and certain injuries make them far more likely. A crushed skull fragment, blood inside the brain tissue, or a very long spell of amnesia all raise the risk. One week of preventive medicine stops early fits, though it cannot prevent epilepsy that starts months later.
steps.tx: **Post-traumatic epilepsy** (seizure disorder after head injury) risk peaks with depressed fractures, intracerebral haematomas and prolonged amnesia. **One week** (seven days) of **phenytoin** (older seizure drug) or **levetiracetam** (newer seizure drug) after severe injury prevents early seizures but not late epilepsy, so prophylaxis stops at **7 days** (seven days) without further fits.
